title: Asma's belt
hook: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma tears her waistband in two to tie the food bags, and is called she of the two belts (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Thawr, two men hidden in the dark with searchers at the mouth. Your line was: two, and Allah the third.

A food bag, a water skin, and no string. That's the whole problem in today's story, and it happens in a house in Mecca on the night two men are about to vanish. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr are leaving for Yathrib in secret. Somebody has to pack the food. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr's daughter, Asma, tells us what happened in that kitchen. The meal is ready. The bags are ready. And there's nothing in the house to tie them shut. Today: Asma's belt.
screen: `NO STRING.` → `A SECRET NIGHT.` → `ASMA IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene as Asma tells it. She prepared the journey food for the Prophet and her father. They looked for something to bind the food bag and the water skin, and found nothing. So she said to her father, in effect: by Allah, I can find nothing to tie it with except my waistband. And Abu Bakr answered: then tear it in two. Tie the water skin with one half and the food with the other. She did. And from that night on, she says, she was called dhat al-nitaqayn: she of the two belts. No miracle, no clever plan. A young woman uses the cloth already wrapped around her, and the great journey of the hijrah leaves the house tied shut with half of a waistband. Notice where she's standing, too. The men will be hidden in a cave. Asma is the one still in the city, in the house the searchers will come to. The sirah tells of her carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed, so her part wasn't finished in the kitchen. And her name doesn't remember a speech or a battle. It remembers a quick, practical choice made with what was in reach. Aisha's telling of the night, also in Bukhari, puts it a little differently: Asma cuts a piece of her belt rather than tearing it in two. Both keep the same picture: the bag closed with her own cloth. The road to Medina didn't begin with what anyone wished they had. It began with what was there.
screen: `NOTHING TO TIE THE BAGS.` · `TEAR IT IN TWO.` · `SHE STAYS IN THE CITY.` · `A NAME FOR A PRACTICAL CHOICE.` · then, large: `SHE OF THE TWO BELTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because you don't have the right tool, the right time, or enough of something. Then look at what's actually around you, in your room, your pocket, your day, and ask quietly: what here could tie this bag shut, not perfectly, just well enough to start? If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with what is already in your hands.
Asma's belt. Torn in two on the night of the hijrah to tie the food and the water, it gave Asma her name: she of the two belts. Today's word.
Your line: two belts. A name that lasted, earned with a torn waistband. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Asma bint Abi Bakr's part in the hijrah from Sahih al-Bukhari and know her by the name it gave her: dhat al-nitaqayn, she of the two belts.

chat.says: Why is Abu Bakr's daughter Asma called she of the two belts?
options: She tore her waistband in two to tie the food and water for the hijrah.
She wore two belts as a sign that she had pledged herself to the faith.
She carried two belts' worth of supplies to the cave every night.
chat.meaning: In Bukhari, with nothing to tie the bags, Abu Bakr told her to tear her waistband in two, and the name stuck: dhat al-nitaqayn.

notes: Bukhari numbers 2979, 3905, 3907 cited from memory; confirm.
In 2979 it is Abu Bakr who tells Asma to tear the belt in two; the index hook says Asma tears it. Script follows the hadith wording. Confirm.
'Carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed' is attributed to the sirah; confirm (Ibn Ishaq; Bukhari 3905 names Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr and Amir ibn Fuhayra for the nightly visits).
'A young woman' is descriptive, no age given; confirm appropriate.
